opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that most of the safety evaluation we do today happens on the model in isolation. We take a base or instruction-tuned model, we throw a set of adversarial prompts at it, we measure how often it refuses or produces something harmful, and then we say, okay, this model is "safe" to some degree. But that's almost never how these models are actually used in practice, especially in enterprise settings. In something like financial services, the model is sitting inside a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline. It's being fed documents, search results, internal knowledge bases, and the user's query gets wrapped in all of that context before the model ever sees it.

And what we found is that this changes the safety profile quite dramatically. You can have a model that looks very well-behaved when you test it on its own, and then once you put it in a RAG setup, it becomes noticeably more willing to produce unsafe or inappropriate outputs. Part of that is just that the retrieved context shifts the distribution. The model is now conditioned on long passages of text that might be perfectly benign, but the safety training it received was largely done on short, direct conversational exchanges. So the guardrails that were learned in that setting don't necessarily transfer. The model is in a sense "out of distribution" relative to its alignment training, even if the content itself isn't malicious.

The second piece is that the risks themselves are domain-specific. Generic safety taxonomies focus on things like violence, self-harm, hate speech, which matter, but if you're deploying a system for, say, financial advice or customer interactions at a bank, the things you really care about look different. You care about the model giving unauthorized investment advice, leaking confidential information that came in through retrieval, making misleading statements about products, or running afoul of regulatory requirements. None of that is well captured by off-the-shelf benchmarks or off-the-shelf guardrail models. So if you only evaluate generically, you both miss the risks that actually matter for your use case and you may over-index on risks that aren't that relevant.

So the next step, to me, is to move evaluation and safeguarding much closer to the deployment context. That means testing the full system, retrieval and all, with realistic documents and realistic queries. It means building risk taxonomies that reflect the domain and the regulatory environment you operate in. And it means designing guardrails that sit in the pipeline and understand that context, rather than assuming that a model that passed a generic safety benchmark will stay safe no matter what you wrap around it. Safety is really a property of the system, not just the model, and our evaluation practices need to catch up with that.

r001.rationale: The response says models that appear safe in isolation become more willing to produce unsafe or inappropriate outputs once placed in a RAG setup.

r002.rationale: It says safety training may not transfer to long retrieved passages, but its proposed next steps are deployment-context evaluation and pipeline guardrails. It does not identify making safety alignment more robust to input variations as a research opportunity.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I think about it is that most of the safety evaluation work that's been done on language models, and most of the benchmarks that people cite, look at the model in isolation. You take the base model, or the instruction-tuned model, you send it a prompt, and you measure whether it refuses something it should refuse, or whether it says something toxic, or whatever the property is. And that's useful, but it's not actually how most of these systems get deployed, especially in enterprise settings.

In practice, what people are building is retrieval-augmented systems. There's a query, you go retrieve some documents from a corpus, you stuff those documents into the context window along with some instructions, and then the model generates an answer. And what we found when we looked at this closely is that the behavior of the model changes quite a bit once you put it into that context. The safeguards that were trained in at the model level are not necessarily robust to having a bunch of retrieved text in the prompt. Sometimes the model becomes more permissive, because the presence of documents sort of signals "this is a legitimate information-seeking task," and the model goes along with things it would have otherwise declined. And sometimes you get the opposite, where the retrieved content introduces unsafe material that wasn't in the query at all, and the model happily summarizes it.

So the gap is really between where we evaluate and where the risk actually materializes. If I'm a company deploying one of these systems, the thing I care about is not whether the base model passes some red-teaming benchmark. It's whether my system, with my documents, with my prompt template, with my particular retrieval setup, behaves safely for my users. And the model-level eval just doesn't tell you that.

The other piece is that the taxonomy of harms is different in a RAG setting. A lot of the safety work has been oriented around things like, will the model help someone build a weapon, or will it produce hateful content. Those matter. But when you're in a domain like finance, which is where I spend a lot of my time, the risks look different. It's things like, is the model confidently presenting information that isn't supported by the retrieved documents? Is it mixing up two entities? Is it giving what amounts to financial advice when it shouldn't? Those are the failures that actually cause harm in a deployment, and they're basically invisible to a general-purpose safety benchmark.

So I think the next step is really twofold. One, build evaluation setups that mirror the deployment configuration, so you're testing the system and not just the model. And two, think about safeguards that operate at that system level too, because you have more levers there. You can filter at retrieval time, you can check the output against the retrieved sources, you can be a lot more targeted than you can be by just trying to train everything into the weights. That's where I think the field needs to go if we want these things to actually be trustworthy in the places they're being used.

astra-6.text:
I think the key issue is that the model in isolation isn’t the system that people actually use. In a RAG application, behavior depends on what gets retrieved, how that information is presented to the model, and what the model is asked to do with it. So a good score on a general benchmark doesn’t necessarily tell you whether that application will be reliable or safe.

For example, if the system produces an incorrect answer, did the retriever fail to find the relevant information, or did the model misinterpret information that was right there? Those are different failure modes, and they require different interventions. You also have to consider what happens when retrieved content is contradictory or contains instructions that the model shouldn’t follow.

That’s why I see evaluation and safeguards moving closer to the deployment context. You want to test the whole system on realistic tasks, understand where it fails, and put safeguards at the points where they can actually help. And you want to keep doing that as the documents, the model, and the way people use the application change.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key point is that what we care about is how a model behaves in the system where people actually use it. A benchmark can tell you something about the model in isolation, but in a RAG application, its behavior also depends on what gets retrieved, how that information is presented, and what the user is asking it to do.

For example, if the system gives a wrong answer, was the relevant information missing from the retrieved documents, or did the model fail to use information that was there? Those are different problems, and they require different interventions. You also have to consider what happens when retrieved content contains instructions that the model shouldn’t follow.

So evaluating closer to deployment gives us a way to test those interactions and make safeguards more specific to the application. Can the system support its answer with the available evidence? Can it recognize when that evidence isn’t sufficient? Those are much more useful questions for a deployed application than whether the model gets a good score on a general benchmark.
